takeaway: In heart failure, SGLT2 inhibitors lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality versus placebo, and in HFrEF they reduce cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation/urgent visits by about 25% [1].
clinicalQuestion: Should an SGLT2 inhibitor be started for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
background: Individual trials were not all powered for mortality. This meta-analysis pools them [1].
studyDesign: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials.
population: 20,241 patients in 15 randomised trials; 10,594 (52.3%) received an SGLT2 inhibitor.
primaryOutcome: Mortality and the composite of cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalisation, or urgent heart-failure visit.
mainFindings: All-cause mortality HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.79–0.94; p=0.0007). Cardiovascular mortality HR 0.86 (0.78–0.96; p=0.006). In the HFrEF subgroup the composite of cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalisation/urgent visit had a 25% relative reduction (OR 0.75; 95% CI 0.62–0.91). The composite was also reduced across sex, age, race, eGFR, and NYHA class subgroups reported by the authors [1].
clinicalMeaning: For a patient with HFrEF, the pooled trials support starting an SGLT2 inhibitor to reduce worsening heart failure and cardiovascular death, not only glucose [1].
limitations: The HFrEF result is a subgroup odds ratio. The paper pools more than one ejection-fraction phenotype, so it is not a single HFrEF trial [1].
bottomLine: Yes: start an SGLT2 inhibitor in HFrEF on the basis of a pooled reduction in mortality and a 25% relative reduction in the HFrEF composite [1].
practiceImplication: Do not withhold an SGLT2 inhibitor in HFrEF solely because the patient does not have diabetes; the meta-analysis is of heart-failure trials [1].
trustRationale: Pooled randomised trials with a prespecified-looking HFrEF subgroup, but not one dedicated trial.
quizFocusPoints: indication is heart failure, not only diabetes
whatNotToOverclaim: Do not quote DAPA-HF's primary hazard ratio as if this paper reported it separately.
An in-hospital acute-heart-failure trial is a different question.
